articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction. articles.title: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neuronal excitability is a nonlinear phenomenon, and the complexity of spiking experimental traces sometimes looks defeating. The present paper takes the view point that excitability is a neuromodulated property, and aims to demonstrate that the neuromodulation of spiking is amenable to the classical linear analysis tools of control theory. We illustrate the value of linear feedback analysis as an alternative to bifurcation analysis in the simple yet classical example of spiking modulation by the A-type potassium current.

articles.title: Path-dependent triage: Early judgments lead conversational AI chatbots to miss mental-health emergencies
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.09647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People increasingly bring mental-health concerns to consumer AI chatbots. In these conversations, clinically relevant information rarely arrives all at once. Instead, it unfolds over multiple turns, often in response to the questions the chatbot asks. articles.title: Scientists wipe out deadly brain tumors in every mouse tested with new cancer therapy
articles.summary: Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a powerful new cancer therapy that remains inactive until it reaches the brain, where it switches on to attack deadly tumors. The engineered immune cells, called B-SYNC CAR-T cells, completely eliminated diffuse midline glioma (DMG), an aggressive childhood brain cancer that is almost always fatal within a year, in two mouse models.

articles.title: Waiting to have sex linked to lower depression risk later in life
articles.summary: Waiting until older ages to have sex for the first time is associated with a lower risk of adult depression. A new study indicates this reduced risk is largely driven by higher educational achievement and increased household income.

articles.title: AI chatbots can flip-flop on false claims when users keep repeating them
articles.summary: What happens when a user keeps insisting that a square has five sides? A study of seven large language models found that sustained conversational pressure exposed weaknesses that single-question tests can miss.

articles.title: Toddler temperament is linked to common DNA variations, large genetic study finds
articles.summary: Why do some toddlers charge into a room of strangers while others hang back? A study of tens of thousands of children links early temperament to common DNA variations that overlap with those tied to ADHD and autism.

articles.title: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
articles.summary: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.

articles.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
articles.summary: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.
